title: Domain-Driven Design: ubiquitous language and bounded contexts

videos.script: Ask three people in a library what a book is, and you get three answers. {{three}} The cataloguer means a work with an ISBN. The lending desk means a copy with a barcode. The person who orders from suppliers means a line on an invoice. All three are right. This lesson is about building software that lets them stay right. It is the strategic half of Domain-Driven Design. {{ddd}} First, when it is worth the trouble at all, and when a simple form will do. {{when}} Then the words. A glossary made with the librarians, and code that uses it, so a stack trace reads like the desk. {{words}} Then which parts of the library deserve your best work, and which you should simply buy. {{parts}} Then the boundaries where one meaning of book stops and another starts, and a map of how those parts depend on each other. {{map}} You will write a small layer that keeps a national catalogue's odd format out of your own code. {{acl}} And last, a workshop with sticky notes on a wall, where most of this is found in an afternoon. {{wall}}
